utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to you. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are here. Representation is as yesterday. That's -- I only notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic. Otherwise, everyone else is -- wait a minute. Thank you. Before we start, Mr. McCloskey and, for that matter, also the other Defence teams, although to a lesser degree, the Miletic Defence team have filed a public motion, dated -- it's filed on the 14th of September, but for some reason it's dated 2nd June, for admission of relevant information -- you filed two motions yesterday, one we don't need to mention; we'll deal with it in due course. And the other one is for admission of some documents. Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this public motion is a translation of a motion that was filed on the 2nd of June. It's not a new motion. It is the translation of a former one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it. Okay, thank you. We have concluded yesterday with the Pandurevic Defence team closing arguments. Our understanding was that today we would proceed with further submissions from you, Mr. McCloskey. Then we will have statements from two of the accused. Mr. Gosnell, I saw your microphone switched on. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just before we commence with the Prosecution's rebuttal argument, a very brief submission to ensure that we're all on the same page as to the contours of what should be contained in a rebuttal argument. And in that regard, I commend to you a quotation from Judge Liu in the Naletilic case from page 16820, and Judge Liu in that case said: "Pursuant to Rule 86 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, tomorrow morning we will have the rebuttal argument. I would like to remind both parties that in this respect, this Tribunal has adopted very strict criteria for this procedure. According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, the rebuttal argument must be related to the significant issues arising directly out of the Defence final brief and closing argument which could not have reasonably been anticipated. The Prosecution could not repeat what has already been said in its final brief and closing argument with the sole purpose to reinforce its case." So, Your Honours, we're simply submitting to you that rebuttal should be restricted in its purposes, and that you should bear in mind, in determining how broad their scope for rebuttal is, how much time we have to prepare any rejoinder that we might wish to submit to you. So we're not making any specific submissions beyond that. We're quite sure that the Prosecutor will bear this in mind and govern himself according to that standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I still consider it almost a storm in a tea cup, considering that after one whole week of oral submissions in the form of closing arguments, the Prosecution has indicated that it only needs about 15 minutes. But in any case, of course, that is taken into account, Mr. Gosnell, and I now give the floor to Mr. McCloskey for his rebuttal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. I would -- my first comments will be of a legal -- of a very short legal nature. We have heard from some of the Defences, I think it was Miletic and we've heard a bit from Pandurevic, suggesting that material documents, things such as perhaps Directive 4 or the six strategic objectives, or some of the material from Operation Proboj generated by the Zvornik Brigade, could not be used by you in your deliberations, except for, as Mr. Haynes said, credibility. Well, I would direct the parties, and, of course, the Court, I'm sure, is familiar with this since it's fundamental to your deliberations, the Stakic appeal, which if you look at paragraphs 105 to 136, clearly allows the Trial Chamber to look at evidence, and that evidence is probative, that may be before or outside the time-frame of the indictment, for things such as context; paragraph 119: "... 'the authority of the appellant during the relevant time-period' and his mens rea (paragraph 120); 'the development of the common purpose' and the 'role played by the appellant,' (paragraph 123); 'the mens rea of the crime of persecutions,' 'the intent to discriminate against non-Serbs,' 'the character of the accused,' and 'the appellant's "real intentions and feelings" about Muslims during the period of the indictment' (paragraph 126); and again, 'the Trial Chamber did not abuse its discretion ...,'" in reviewing these matters. Also, as you'll recall, Mr. Haynes spent quite a bit of time criticising the Prosecution for not putting its case to the accused. I believe we've touched on this a bit before, but it's important to take a good look at the Krajisnik appeal judgement of 17 March 2009, referring to the Karera appeal judgement of February 2009. In paragraph 369 of the Krajisnik appeal judgement, the ICTR appeals -- it quotes the ICTR Appeals Chamber in the Karera case, referring to Rule 90(G)(ii), and says this: "When an accused testifies in his own defence, he is well aware of the context of the Prosecution's questions and the Prosecution's case, insofar he has received sufficient notice of the charges and the material facts supporting them." It went on to state that: "The ICTR Appeals Chamber, therefore, found that Rule 90(G)(ii) of the Rules was not intended to apply to an accused testifying as a witness in his own case. The Appeals Chamber agrees with this reasoning for the purposes of Rule 90(H)(ii) of the Rules." And it went on to say: "In the present case, the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that, when taking the stand to testify in his own defence, Krajisnik was well aware of the context of the Prosecution's questions and of the Prosecution's case against him. In particular, the indictment, the Prosecution pre-trial brief, and the witness lists issued in accordance with Rule 65 ter, as well as his presence during the trial proceedings as a whole, informed Krajisnik, the last person testifying for the Defence, of the case against him. In these circumstances, the Appeals Chamber concluded that the Prosecution was not required to put the nature of its case to Krajisnik when cross-examining him." It goes on in paragraph 371: "Amicus curiae also argues that, with regard to matters about which Krajisnik testified, and the Prosecution did not cross-examine him, the Trial Chamber was bound to accept Krajisnik's account." Well, the Appeals Chamber - I won't read it to you - but goes on and says the Trial Chamber is not bound to do that just because the Prosecution doesn't hit him with a particular part of their case or a particular document; that it's the Trial Chamber's discretion to weigh all the evidence, and I'm sure you'll do that. And if I didn't ask the general about a document related to fuel, I'm sure you'll balance that, if that's an important determination for you. No concern about that. But that is the correct law of the Tribunal. Now, counsel for Borovcanin. I will mainly limit my remarks to the area of commission by omission, but counsel for Borovcanin criticised the interview with Mr. Borovcanin, basically said he wasn't given a chance to explain things. Well, I think you know that interview, and we know how thorough the Borovcanin Defence can be, and had there been any untoward comments or problems in that interview, we would have heard them loud and clear on the audio. So it was a fair interview, it was a just interview. Mr. Borovcanin and I had two different interviews, good discussions, tough discussions, clear discussions. He had no problems. He told jokes during the interview. You know this Prosecution. You know this Prosecutor perhaps better than he knows himself, after three years. You don't see any of that kind of nonsense being played here. Okay. Now, Mr. Gosnell suggested that this issue of Mr. Borovcanin's defence, whether he went to Zvornik or towards Zvornik, was just nitpicking on the part of the Prosecutor; that when we clearly tell you what -- and it is in his statement that he said he went to Zvornik, that that doesn't really matter because what really matters is that he was able to tell us about his troops along the road. Well, that doesn't work because, as is clear in this case from the testimony of Mr. Ruez, the Petrovic video of his troops and himself along the road has been in the custody of the Prosecution since 1995. Mr. Borovcanin would have known that and would have had to speak about his troops and himself being on the road. What he had to do is come up with a story to explain it. And the Borovcanin Defence is suggesting to you that Borovcanin was just telling us he was going towards Zvornik, towards Zvornik, and that he'd been ordered to stop along the road. Well, he told me very clearly in his interview, at least three times, he was going to Zvornik. Now, the Defence is correct in that there were a couple of translation errors, and as you know, in an interview like this, they're not really translated. The transcript of the English is transcribed, and the transcript of the B/C/S is transcribed, and sometimes the interpreter will make a mistake. "To" and "towards" are obviously very closely-related words, and sometimes they flip back and forward in the B/C/S, and it should have been "towards" sometimes when it was said "to." But the vast majority of the times, they got it right and it was "to." But just to absolutely clear this issue up, I want to go over with you the three key points to show us that he was telling me he was going to Zvornik. In the February interview, P02852, page 73, lines 5 through 10, I ask him: "So what did you do with the troops that you had? Where did you go?" "We started towards Zvornik." "And what were your particular orders? Where were you supposed to go? Zvornik is a big municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVCANIN SAYS
utterances.text: "I was supposed to go to the command of the Zvornik Brigade to take over my task of duty." "And who told you to do that?" "General Mladic." Very clear, he's going to the command of the Zvornik Brigade, not just towards Zvornik. Also at 2852, a few pages later, 78, line 23 to 26, I say: "Okay. So when your troops went up towards Zvornik, it was their job to secure that route?" Borovcanin: "First task was to go to Zvornik, but that order to secure the communications changed the way we were supposed to be engaged." So, again, the first task was to go to Zvornik, and then he comes up with this wild defence that he got hung out in limbo because he couldn't go on the road. But now the third time, to make it absolutely clear, this is now in the March interview, and you can tell, by reading this, that Mr. Borovcanin is a very intelligent man and he has gone into this well prepared, and he's continuing the same theme. So I say: "So you've received orders to go to a very dangerous area, where the Muslim column is going, but you don't receive any detailed intel reports, except for what Mladic told you?" Borovcanin: "My order was to go to Zvornik and report to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and be at his disposal for the defence of Zvornik, because the members of the Zvornik Brigade moved towards Zepa and the town of Zvornik was not protected." Then he goes on to describe how the road got cut and he couldn't make it. So this was definitely on the 12th that he was talking about. And that is not nitpicking; it's crucial. It's crucial to his defence, as he gave it to me in that interview, because that's the only way he gets out of being in command of Dusko Jevic's troops, the ones that are doing the separating, and that's the only way he gets out of command of being under General Krstic's command, that -- the troops that were doing the killing and the operation to murder people. And only with this trial and this latest developments has this been reconstructed and changed. And I hear no complaint from anyone, so we must view that as the new version of events. Very important to understand that. Now, Mr. Gosnell also argued strenuously that Mr. Borovcanin did not control and did not have custody of these prisoners at key points, and I want to just briefly go over you, first of all, what precisely they have acknowledged in their brief and then highlight some of the importance of the crucial evidence on this commission by omission, which is, as you know, does not, in the end, final analysis, require custody. But you know that law, and we'll go through the facts. Custody is important. So at paragraph 166 of the final brief, they say: "The 2nd Sekovici Detachment and the 1st PJP Company had been deployed along the road since the previous afternoon, tasked with securing the road and blocking and fighting the ABiH column that was moving north." We agree. "The Prosecution concedes that the column was a legitimate military target. This task necessarily encompassed securing the road and regulating traffic thereon." We agree with that, and that, of course, also allowed the women and children to move freely and be freely kicked out. Then it goes on to say, an important part: "A further necessary incident of that combat function was taking ABiH fighters into detention at the point of surrender and securing them until they could be handed over to the unit responsible for prisoners of war." It goes on to describe that that would be the security branch of the Bratunac Brigade. So there's a clear acknowledgment of what the evidence was, overwhelming, on video, showing, all part of our case, so I won't go through our case. He also acknowledges at paragraph 365 that he took prisoners and guarded them at Sandici, and it says: "The evidence concerning who had custody of Muslim prisoners at various times on the afternoon of the 13th of July has already been analysed in detail." An important part: "Borovcanin's units did take prisoners into custody, where they surrendered along the road, and did participate in guarding them at the Sandici Meadow for at least some period." That's an important acknowledge that is supported by all our evidence, and it makes your job easier. He also acknowledged that one of his key commanders, Cuturic, would have been working with Momir Nikolic, and that is in paragraph 189 of their final brief, and states: "The task of Mr. Borovcanin's units, in addition to blocking and fighting the column, was to ensure security along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road. Cuturic's role in closing the road flowed directly from this responsibility." And here's the important part: "Of course, he would have coordinated with Momir Nikolic or others about the need to close traffic for the purpose of marching a column of detainees down the road." So he is acknowledging that he would have been coordinating with Momir Nikolic or others about this key point. And we know Momir Nikolic was going up and down the road that day with an APC, calling out people to come join the UN. And in paragraph 9 of Momir Nikolic's statement of facts, he says this, for the 13th of July: "While I was in Potocari, I met Dusko Jevic and told him to pass an order to his units which were on the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, that all the captured Muslims be transported to Bratunac." So, yes, Cuturic would be dealing with Nikolic. Nikolic is dealing with Cuturic, through Jevic, all under the command of Borovcanin. They're working together in this system, in this operation, which I've already thoroughly described to you. So I just want to clear up this issue about how the executions began, whether it was organised part under Boro's orders or -- Borovcanin's orders, excuse me, or related to some sort of escape attempt, which it was certainly not. Mr. Gosnell said that you cannot hear detonations or sounds - I don't remember his exact words on that point - over the trial video, that -- where we said you could hear them. Well, I'm not going to play them for you, but you can go to -- in the trial video, go to two hours and fifty-one minutes and forty-eight seconds, and go to two hours, fifty-two minutes and three seconds, and you will hear two loud, distinct noises while Petrovic is filming in the area of Sandici. At the same time, you'll be hearing loud automatic gun-fire coming from the area. And the only evidence we have of any kind of gun-fire or fighting in the afternoon on 13 July along that road is the Kravica warehouse. Now, we can't possibly discount to you that gun-fire was not heard, somebody shot into the woods or something like that, but when you listen to the -- when you go over the evidence, it's -- the fact that this gun-fire and what people hear all happens after the road was closed is very telling on what was going on. Even in the statements to Mr. Borovcanin -- to me, he said, on page 285 -- excuse me, in Prosecution's 2853, page 63: "So when someone turned on his Motorola," and remember he's got a Motorola that we see in his car; it's always going to be on, as a commander, and he's also got, as you saw, a hand-held mic that would be attached to the car, and that's always going to be on, so I'll start over: "So when someone turned on his Motorola, I was able to hear shooting and detonations. I tried to reach some of my commanders that were there because I wanted to know what was going on. I believed that the police got attacked somewhere." "Stupar," and later he says: "Stupar, the commander of the Sekovici, I heard him, so I tried to get an answer from him. I asked him what was going on, what's the problem, but he just -- I couldn't get a concrete answer from him. He just kept saying, 'Oh, don't ask, don't ask, something terrible is going on.'" Earlier in the day, Mr. Borovcanin told me that he'd met with his commanders, Stupar, Cuturic, and Pantic, along that road, and here is him acknowledging that he is speaking to Stupar right at the time that these -- something terrible is going on, and he's previously -- just previously to this -- it's impossible to tell how previously, but he has heard detonations and shooting. And after the traffic was stopped for the prisoners, Celic, a MUP member who was along that road, hears hand-grenades. He doesn't give great timing on that, but it's clearly before dark, and it's a time he's hearing gun-fire. So here we have more gun-fire, hand-grenades, after the people are sent there. And I note that our brief suggested Pepic heard hand-grenades as well. That is wrong. Pepic did not say he heard hand-grenades. He heard constant fire -- one-sided firing after the traffic was stopped. So at this point we know that Commander Cuturic is at the warehouse with the prisoners, as is Krsto, and "burnt hands" happens during this, and shooting erupts. And since Stupar -- don't forget Stupar. He is on the radio probably immediately with Borovcanin, so he is very likely there as well, or very close by, and gets there almost immediately. Borovcanin is last seen on the video at Sandici. We believe he would have gone from Sandici directly to Kravica. So they're all very close by. So why is Krsto there? Now, you heard from the opening statement and recent statements of Defence counsel. Let me -- the evidence on that is amazingly sparse and amazingly unreasonable. It should not be something that you need to consider, but I go over with you what it is. It's nothing like what was in the opening statement. Now, clearly, they don't have a burden, but when they get up and tell you that Cuturic took Krsto to go talk to people at the warehouse about a relative that was killed, they should back it up with something. So we put on Milenko Pepic, a MUP officer, and he was cross-examined. I believe it was by Mr. Stojanovic. His question was, at T-13600: "Did Rado Cuturic tell you how it is that Dragicevic, Krsto, ended up in Kravica?" "A. No. "Q. At any point in time, did you obtain information according to which Krsto Dragicevic went there to check whether any of his Muslim neighbours were there, neighbours he could ask about the fate of his brother or cousin who was killed in 1993? "A. I can't say. I don't remember." So leading questions are fine on cross-examination, but as you know, the problem with leading questions is they're good for credibility, they're good for determining credibility, but they're not very good for getting information from a witness. You get information from a lawyer, but not from the witness. "My question was whether after these events, you had heard of such a reason for which Krsto went down there. So I'm not asking you about that evening. I'm asking you about whether you heard about this later." Second try. "A. I can't provide you with a precise answer, but there was some relative of his that was killed, and it's probably for that reason." That's it. A second leading question, and it's probably for that reason. No talk of Cuturic or anything else. Mr. Thayer goes over a similar topic with him and gets a similar sort of non-clear response. And Mr. Thayer's questions on page 13607 to 08: "So my question, sir, is when did you first hear this information or rumour that this Krle had had a relative that was killed at Kravica?" At that point, Mr. Stojanovic objects and says: "Oh, it was Skelani." Mr. Thayer continued, and the witness answered: "I couldn't say when exactly, but perhaps Krle, himself, said something about a relative of his in Skelani who had been killed." Perhaps Krle himself. "As to when this occurred, as to the year, I don't know, but it was during the war. "Q. Do you remember when you heard this information, sir? "A. I can't remember." That's it, that's all they have, and when you balance whether or not Krsto and Cuturic were there in their capacity to guard people, this is what you're balancing it up against, and this is just not reasonable. In addition, the MUP troops had taken these people in custody. They'd surrendered to the MUP troops. They'd taken them into custody. Borovcanin stopped the traffic to help facilitate their movement. Borovcanin's troops held that road, as we know from Celic. He had his people on the other side of the warehouse, from Pepic, who had stopped it. This is his zone, he's in control of this. These people stay in his custody and control. The fact that they're a few metres away, along the road, while they're being escorted down the road perhaps by army guys that they're working with, does not change the custody situation here at all. This is not a situation where they're being taken to a small local prison and Krsto and Cuturic are going to visit somebody that's been in the custody of the county jail, and the state police are off patrolling the highways. No. This is the area held by Mr. Borovcanin, controlled by him, and I've gone over that in detail. I won't -- try not to repeat myself, where necessary, or not necessary. If I could go into private session for just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sure. Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, a Defence witness in the Blagojevic testimony, Ljubisa Simic, which is -- came in, I think, under 92 bis, Exhibit P00092, Exhibit 4D00606, at 7629 to 7630, Simic says, in recounting the story, and I quote: "A policeman who was guarding those people in the -- in the -- okay," and it goes on: "That policeman was killed and then shooting ensued." And to get a final picture of who is there, we go to the words of Mr. Borovcanin himself at P02853 page, 63 to 65, and this is as he's coming up -- he's come back after being summoned back by Stupar. He doesn't say where he's summoned to, which is a little odd, but he says, as he comes up to the Kravica: "I saw -- and I saw police officers that were previously placed along the road. I saw them gathered there. I saw Lukic's unit. They were all together as well, and I saw a large number of bodies of people that were killed in the yard." And that's when Stupar reports to him what happened. I ask him: "How many bodies?" And he says: "I wouldn't dare make an estimate, so large a number, several dozens." And I went on to ask him: "Did you look in the warehouse?" And he said: "So -- well, I can tell you that I looked towards the warehouse, and Pirocanac was near me, and he was taking photographs of -- he was filming the place, and on that footage you can also see the warehouse, but you cannot see what's in the warehouse because it's dark." No mention of closed doors. We were able to agree with the Defence that that statement was not correct of Mr. Borovcanin. But in any event, we have now several dozens dead Muslims at the Kravica warehouse shortly after 5.00 p.m., probably 5.15, 5.20. Krsto is dead. Cuturic has had his hands burned badly. Stupar is there, Borovcanin is there. Other members of Borovcanin's unit are there that were placed along the road, and many, many are yet to die, and there's a huge pile of people. And as you know, when you shoot large numbers of people like this, they don't all die at once; they die slowly many times, that they bleed to death. So there are many, many people that are left to save. And, really, there's one man there at this time that can do that, and that's Ljubisa Borovcanin. And on page 28 -- 2853, 66 through 67, and then -- excuse me, page 72, I ask the question: "Did you make any effort to see if there were any wounded people among the mass of Muslims that had been shot at the warehouse?" Answer, and I quote: "First, my officer was wounded and he needed medical assistance. And whether there were any wounded among the Muslims, I did not want to interfere in that matter." The argument is clear, the facts are clear. You know what that means. He did nothing. He said he goes to the health centre. Pepic says when Cuturic goes to the health centre, Borovcanin is not with him. Someone needs to stay there and sort out the security of these prisoners. There's a security problem. There's been a massive crime. Those several dozens bodies piled there cannot have anything but a massively, massively suspicious nature, at the very least, in looking at this in the best possible view to the accused. You don't need to kill several dozens of people when one guy grabs a gun, and you certainly, under International Law, and what the Defence called, I think, the duty to render assistance or protect, known well in Serbia, he had to do something, both to look after the wounded and to protect the others that were there. He did nothing except ensure that the traffic could be opened when Cuturic came back after the health centre and that women and children could get by this warehouse and not see anything, which meant that he had to help organise the rest of the killings, the covering up of the bodies and the blood with hay. This is what he did, and everyone in that warehouse died that afternoon and early evening, and even into the night. As people twitched and got up, as we know from the witnesses, people were shot into the night. His presence there with his staff, Stupar and other officers, would have also, under the other form of liability, encouraged those that are there to continue killing. And Pepic hears firings continuing when Cuturic goes by him with burned hands on his way to the health centre. He showed a similar disregard when it had to do with the Muslims in Potocari; 2853, page 95. Allistair Graham asked him: "Had all the prisoners been moved out of town by this stage or was this still a problem? "A. I don't know that. I tried not to know." And I ask: "Why?" "Because that was not the thing that was supposed to interest me." And I ask: "What do you mean by that?" "I had enough headaches without that," is his response. I'm not sure any legal term fits that mindset, but the term "deliberate indifference" comes to mind. And then he was asked about the Muslims that were being held in Bratunac and whether he was concerned for their safety, and he said: "I did not think about it. I did not know what might happen to them." And about the separations, he said: "I didn't pay attention to that. I don't know anything." So when you look carefully at the law of Mrksic, the Geneva Conventions, which clearly state the duty, I can't imagine any greater example of an officer that knows full well he has to do something, he has the ability to do something, he does nothing, and hundreds and hundreds die a horrible death. Now I'd like to move on to Pandurevic. I didn't hear too much new in the Pandurevic arguments, and much of this has been discussed in the brief, but there are some matters that I'd like to discuss. And I hope we'll be done within 25 minutes. I can't imagine -- I hope I'll be done by then. Mr. Haynes said that the Prosecution did not comment on the Defence that Pandurevic had no effective control of the Zvornik Brigade. Given that that was an issue hotly contested by all the security teams and put on by Mr. Butler and throughout our case, I'm not sure we were in the same courtroom. But just to clarify it, very briefly, Vinko Pandurevic took over command, actual command, about noon on the 15th of July. He was always, of course, in command of the Zvornik Brigade, and the key factor we know about that we get from Mirko Trivic, that when you're out of your zone with other matters, you're still commander, and if the deputy commander back at home -- he is obligated to be consistent with your commands and with your orders, and if anything new and different of a nature arises, you've got to get a hold of your commander or his commander. And in that regard, you're still the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He tacitly -- he put his brigades, he authorised the murder operation to come to Zvornik, to the Zvornik Brigade. And after that, each soldier that acted in furtherance of that operation was acting under his command. And that is exactly what happened when Vinko Pandurevic got back on noon on the 15th. He became fully informed of the murder operation by his Chief of Staff, by his other officers at the brigade command. And after that, each officer, each soldier that acted in that brigade, could only be under the command of one commander, and that was Vinko Pandurevic. Under the Rules, he's responsible for everything that goes on in subordinate units. It's clearly written in the Rule. He knows it, we know it. He would have had to have been relieved for him not to be in command. Butler said that very early. He was never relieved of command. They probably thought about it when he opened up the column, after his men got killed, but they decided that it was because his men got killed, he opened the column, and they weren't going to relieve him. They needed him too much. He never got relieved. He's the only commander. Even if Krstic or Mladic were there, he would be the commander of the brigade. The orders come down through Mladic -- well, Karadzic, Mladic, Krstic, down through to the brigade, to Pandurevic. They're existing when he gets there. When he allows his troops to continue in that, instead of putting an end to it, they are under his command. He is actively commanding them. And that's when I go through the three processes of intent that I talked to you about, everything that he did voluntarily against his duty. So to make that absolutely clear, that is our case. The 15th of July intercept makes that clear. As I've said, I won't go over the entire argument, but it's absolutely clear that as Krstic ticks off the brigade commanders that Beara needs to go to in order to try to get more troops, it's clear that not even Beara -- and Beara says if he -- you know, If I had those other troops that had been promised me three days ago by Mladic, Beara, even with Mladic's order, putting it in front of Krstic's nose, Give me the troops that Mladic said I could get, Krstic listed off the brigades that he could go to to try to get them. He did not mention Pandurevic. Why not? Krstic and Pandurevic had just met that morning at the -- before Pandurevic was sent back to Zvornik. There is no doubt at that point that Krstic would have fully informed Pandurevic, perhaps not as fully as Pandurevic would have liked, but would have given him the guts of what was going on up there in his brigade, and I'm sure Pandurevic said, You better get some people to help take part in this operation, both militarily and the other one, because I'm not going up there, you know, and get my head handed to me. So when Beara calls an hour or two later, you don't see Krstic saying, Oh, yeah, talk to Pandurevic to get more troops. Pandurevic's guys are max'd out. Look in our brief about what they're doing at that point. I'll go over it briefly, but they are completely max'd out. So that little window into reality is a very important one, and remember where Beara is when he's having that conversation. All right. The other thing Mr. Haynes said that we never spoke of is the zone of responsibility. Well, the zone of responsibility must be mentioned in countless numbers of Zvornik Brigade reports. It's mentioned in many places. The -- it's uncontested that the corps has a zone of responsibility that's defined by specific lines. It's the same in the brigade. We did not make a big issue of it - Butler mentions it briefly - because the crux of the issue is this: They're suggesting that because he's not responsible for the areas that aren't on the front, he's not responsible for the schools. How can that be? Let me outline. We know that on the 13th of July, Drago Nikolic, and MPs under the command of Dragan Obrenovic, took over the Orahovac school, and the authority -- under the authority -- the only authority they have to do that is under the authority of the Zvornik Brigade and the command. The same thing happened at the Petkovci school. The commander and deputy commander, Marko Milosevic, Ostoja Stanisic, were informed from the duty office who was -- this thing was getting run out of the duty office, as you know, that there would be prisoners there and Beara would be there. So that school was literally across the street from the command post, and the officers from that -- or the soldiers from that battalion had to clean up bodies and trucks, at a very minimum, at a very minimum. The Rocevic school, Sreco Acimovic, himself, had to go get the keys with someone, and they actually got the school themselves, based on communications from security, from Drago Nikolic. That's the Zvornik Brigade, Drago Nikolic acting under the authority of his commander at the time. And then we heard about the soldiers, the security officer of the 1st Battalion that also had to go get the Kula school and take it and put all its soldiers there. Zone of responsibility? These guys have taken these schools. They have to be responsible for them and the prisoners they put in them. That's a complete red herring. Now, Mr. Haynes went over his, I think, 12 or 13 points, and I'm sure you know that I could match him point for point, but I'm not going to do that because that's in the brief. But there is another section where he answers -- he asks certain questions and provides some answers, and I think it goes to the issue of suggesting the alternatives on why Obrenovic didn't tell Pandurevic about the prisoners and the executions. And the answers that he gave are not reasonable to an extreme, and so I think they help highlight the extremity of their -- the extreme nature of their point. The first question he asks is that once -- they suggest that once Drago Nikolic and Obrenovic know about this operation on the 13th and 14th, Vinko doesn't need to know. Pandurevic absolutely needs to know this when he gets there. One of the main things he needs to know this about is you saw the terrible burden that each of his battalion commanders were under. Lazar Ristic spelled it out. He was worried about his soldiers finding out there was hundreds of Muslims in their community, and if soldiers find out that their children and their families are at risk from hundreds of Muslims kept in bizarre circumstances, being shot, Rocevic, remember, a civilian got shot, a whole group came down from Pilica complaining about the people there, this is a terrible threat that the battalion commanders are having to deal with, that the word gets out, that the soldiers start getting up and leaving the lines, when -- can you imagine Vinko Pandurevic, at the forward command post, and catches people leaving the lines, and it's reported to him, Ah, he's leaving the lines because he's heard there are hundreds of prisoners located at schools. He's got to go back and save his family. Vinko Pandurevic would have the head of anyone who didn't tell him that before he goes out to the IKM. That threatens the entire brigade, it threatens the entire town of Zvornik. He has to know that, that that is a major security threat. He had to know because of all the resources. Could you imagine Vinko Pandurevic getting on to the 1st Battalion and saying, I need -- I need 20 men to help fill a gap in the line. You can bet the deputy that's there, or the security, whoever picks it up, and said, Well, I'd like to be able to send them to you, and I will, but it's going to take me some time to get the 20 guys and find somebody else to guard the people at the Kula school. Pandurevic now has to go look for -- elsewhere. He would be livid if nobody had told him about that and his lack of resources. The same goes with the engineering unit. If he needs engineering equipment to go block a road, fill a trench, build up the trenches, he has to know, before he goes out in harm's way, what resources, what men, are going to be taken away from him and what effect it's going to have on him. He absolutely has to know. The other point he says is -- Mr. Haynes says: "Obrenovic had nothing to tell." My god. From the 13th and the 14th, and everything that had gone on, as I said, the different threats at the different schools, the prisoners that had been killed, the need to take care of people. How about the fact that 2.000 people had already been murdered? Nothing like that had ever happened in this war. Do you think that was a secret that was being held from the commander that needed to know the most? Absolutely not. Had nothing to tell. It's outrageous. He may not have had the opportunity -- Obrenovic may not have had the opportunity to tell this to Pandurevic. Well, they were at the command together. This isn't a position where they're in a trench, getting shelled, and they're trying to save themselves. They're at the command post. There are hallways, there are office to dip into. Opportunity galore. Obrenovic may have thought it was not worth telling him. Well, for the reasons I've gone over, Obrenovic had to tell him. Not worth telling him? Had this happened -- something like this happened in other armies, in other wars, it's grounds to be shot. And if Obrenovic had sent Vinko Pandurevic out to the front-lines without telling him this information, it would be a serious -- very serious security threat and it would put Obrenovic in very, very deep trouble. Obrenovic may have been afraid to tell him. This is not going to be good news to Vinko Pandurevic. If he doesn't know clearly all the details at that point, yes, he is going to be angry, but he's going to be a hell of a lot angrier if you surprise him. I can't imagine how angry he would be if that gets surprised, after he's at the IKM or finds out later. He just happens to find out after everybody is dead and buried on the 16th and 17th. Outrageous. Baljkovica, very briefly. Remember, when you -- if you look at this issue, to determine Vinko Pandurevic's intent. I know we've all been here too long, and I know when Mr. Haynes says only ten dead, he doesn't really mean that. But look at any commander that's lost troops in Afghanistan. Look at General Dannatt. They feel these deaths, these Serb men that are dying. They feel every one of them. And had that column been open the day before, when it was being pushed by Vasic and others, those ten men would probably be alive today. So, yeah, those ten men that he is acknowledging knowing about, that's a lot of men, that's a lot of lives. That's Serb lives that could have been saved if they had just let them through, not to mention the hundreds of Muslims that charged that trench with no weapons and got butchered to get home. And don't forget the Muslims had tanks along that front-line that could reach Zvornik. They also had very heavy artillery that could reach Zvornik. Zvornik had the same thing. Early on, we saw -- I think it was 92 or 93, a Muslim shell hit the centre town and killed a little girl. Well, Vinko Pandurevic has his hands tied by mutual-assured destruction. He can't just lay back and start shelling the hell out of everybody, because then the Muslims do the same thing. They can get Celopek, they can get down-town Zvornik. They can turn each other to rubble. They couldn't do that. So the Baljkovica story is outrageous and needs a little reality. One last point, a point that Mr. Haynes stressed, Vinko Pandurevic stressed. Pandurevic said: "Whose ever life depended upon me, they survived." Now, can we go to P0329, put it up on the screen: "Whose ever life depended upon me, they survived." Well, when Vinko Pandurevic gets to the Zvornik Brigade at 12.00 noon, everybody at the Rocevic school is still alive. Everybody at the Pilica Cultural Centre is alive. Everybody at the Kula school is alive. Well, I shouldn't say "everybody." There's dead people at all these places that have died various awful ways, but most of them are still alive. And look what he says, after he describes the combat situation: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area." Now, that is uncontested. He is acknowledging it is a burden on the brigade, on his command, of the large number of prisoners distributed throughout all the schools. He knows he's got large numbers of prisoners distributed throughout the schools. They're all in his battalions. His battalion commanders are suffering from having to put up with this awful murder operation. He knows it. There it is. By the morning of 17 July, they're all dead. By the evening of 17 -- 18 July, they're all buried. They all depended on Vinko Pandurevic for survival. He chose not to allow them to survive. It was his choice, not Beara's, Drago Nikolic; Vinko Pandurevic. And when he allowed his troops from the brigade command, to the logistics, to the security, to the battalion commands, to the soldiers, the drivers, to continue taking part in this, he willfully joined a genocide, one that will not long soon be forgotten. Thank you.
